---
title: "Wind does not explain mountain pine beetle refugia: a specification artefact across 1,776 m of relief"
author:
  - name: Seamus Murphy
    orcid: 0000-0002-1792-0351
    email: seamusrobertmurphy@gmail.com
    affiliation: "Independent Researcher, Nelson, British Columbia, Canada"
abstract: >
  Mass attack by mountain pine beetle (Dendroctonus ponderosae Hopkins) on lodgepole pine
  (Pinus contorta Douglas ex Loudon) is coordinated by an airborne pheromone plume, so refugia
  are hypothesised to form where stands are thin enough for wind to disrupt that signal, a
  mechanism proposed repeatedly and never entered into a model. We test it across 168 km2 of
  inventoried forest and 1,776 m of relief in southeastern British Columbia, combining an
  aerial overview survey of beetle-caused mortality from 1999 to 2015 with inventory host
  attributes and Global Wind Atlas speed at 10 m. Attack is unimodal, peaking
  near 1,430 m. Below 1,900 m that peak is the distribution of the host; above it, attack
  halves while cover holds, so coding host as cover alone overstates the result. Attack rises
  monotonically with stand quadratic mean diameter, from 15 to 41 per cent, stepping most
  steeply at the 25 cm source-sink threshold the species' bionomics predicts, and the share
  of stands above that threshold falls four-fold at the top of the gradient.
  Conditioning on the full host set removes about a quarter of the suppression. We find no
  wind effect.
  Orthogonalised against a linear elevation term, wind is the strongest negative predictor in
  host-bearing stands and clears the interval test at every severity threshold above trace,
  but a unimodal response leaves elevation's curvature inside that term, and refitting
  elevation as a quadratic or a spline collapses the coefficient everywhere. The signal is a
  specification artefact, and the atlas does not report the quantity the insect responds to,
  flight being arrested by instantaneous below-canopy speeds near 2 m per second. Thermal
  alternatives survive. A Landsat red-stage classification built to replace the survey fails
  against it. Elevation explains 0.63 of the wind surface's variance landscape-wide and 0.80
  within a 2 by 4 km clip.
keywords:
  - bark beetle
  - disturbance refugia
  - pheromone disruption
  - Landsat classification
  - spatial block bootstrap
  - collinearity
date: today
format:
  docx:
    prefer-html: true
    reference-doc: ../04.references/style-formal.docx
    highlight-style: pygments
    number-sections: true
execute:
  eval: true

  comment: NA
always_allow_html: true

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| echo: true
#| output: false

## Every quantity in this manuscript is computed here at render time.
## patchwork is loaded for its `+` operator on ggplots (@fig-gradient), which is
## why no patchwork function appears by name anywhere below.
pkgs <- c("terra","knitr","kableExtra","ggplot2","dplyr","patchwork","tibble","kernlab",
          "sf","ggspatial","tidyterra","ggrepel","rnaturalearth","scales","parallel")
invisible(lapply(pkgs, function(p) library(p, character.only = TRUE)))
## dpi 300 is the Elsevier minimum for a combination line/halftone figure.
## error = FALSE on purpose: in a manuscript whose every number is computed at
## render time, a chunk that fails quietly while downstream inline expressions
## carry stale values is the one failure this design exists to prevent.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, error = FALSE,
                      comment = NA, dpi = 500, fig.align = "center",
                      cache.path = "_cache/", autodep = TRUE, cache.lazy = FALSE)
## Caching is opt-in per chunk and is applied only to the model-fitting chunks, which
## between them refit the block bootstrap roughly four thousand times per render.
## `autodep = TRUE` makes knitr read each chunk's globals and invalidate a cached
## chunk when any chunk that created those globals changes, so a cached result
## cannot outlive the data it was computed from. That guarantee is the only reason
## caching is acceptable in a manuscript whose whole design is that no number can go
## stale. It is not absolute: knitr tracks R objects, not files on disk. If an input
## raster or CSV changes without its reading chunk changing, delete `_cache/` and
## render again. `make clean-cache` does that, and the submission render should
## always be run from an empty cache.
knitr::dep_auto()
options(scipen = 999)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
          theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
                plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10)))

B_BOOT   <- 150L    # spatial block bootstrap replicates
BLOCK    <- 40L     # block side in cells (40 x 25.1 m ~= 1 km)
OUTBREAK <- 1999:2015
## The elevation above which conditioning on host stops removing the decline.
## It is a band edge of the 200 m banding in @tbl-gradient and is quoted in the
## prose, so it is defined once here rather than typed into each comparison.
ALPINE   <- 1900
```

```{r}
#| label: map-furniture
#| echo: true

## Cartography shared by the four map figures, defined once here so each figure can
## sit in the section it documents instead of being grouped at the end of Materials
## for want of its furniture. Graticule, EPSG, north arrow, bar scale and a
## representative fraction quoted against a stated printed width are set once and

clip_src <- rast(dpath("beetle_stages", "Beetle.Oubteak.2005.tif"))
clip_sf  <- st_as_sf(project(as.polygons(ext(clip_src), crs = crs(clip_src)), crs(G)))
grid_sf  <- st_as_sf(as.polygons(ext(G), crs = crs(G)))
ev <- as.vector(ext(G)); gw <- ev["xmax"] - ev["xmin"]; gh <- ev["ymax"] - ev["ymin"]
## Graticule and axis ticks are drawn in the same coordinate reference system the
## panel declares, so the CRS named beneath each title is the CRS the reader is
## reading off the frame. Ticks are metres divided by 1,000; the subtitle says so.
km_lab  <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f", x / 1000)
sub_utm <- "EPSG:32611 WGS 84 / UTM 11N; ticks in km"
sub_alb <- "EPSG:3005 NAD83 / BC Albers; ticks in km"

map_theme <- theme_bw(base_size = 8) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_line(colour = "grey70", linewidth = .25, linetype = "dotted"),
        axis.title = element_blank(), axis.text = element_text(size = 6, colour = "grey25"),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 8.5, margin = margin(b = 1)),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 6, colour = "grey35", margin = margin(b = 3)),
        legend.key.width = unit(3.2, "mm"), legend.key.height = unit(7, "mm"),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 6.5), legend.text = element_text(size = 6))

north <- annotation_north_arrow(location = "tr", which_north = "true",
  height = unit(6, "mm"), width = unit(5, "mm"),
  pad_x = unit(1.2, "mm"), pad_y = unit(1.2, "mm"),
  style = north_arrow_orienteering(text_size = 5, line_width = .6,
    fill = c("white", "grey20"), text_col = "grey20"))

## White plates behind the north arrow and the clip label. Without them the arrow is
## unreadable over the dark end of the wind ramp and the label collides with the
## severity polygons.
plate <- annotate("rect", xmin = ev["xmin"] + .885*gw, xmax = ev["xmax"],
                  ymin = ev["ymax"] - .115*gh, ymax = ev["ymax"],
                  fill = "white", alpha = .72, colour = NA)
clip_layer <- geom_sf(data = clip_sf, fill = NA, colour = "#C0392B", linewidth = .45)
study <- list(coord_sf(crs = 32611, datum = st_crs(32611), expand = FALSE,
                       xlim = ev[c("xmin","xmax")], ylim = ev[c("ymin","ymax")]),
              scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(520000, 530000, 5000), labels = km_lab),
              scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(5440000, 5450000, 5000), labels = km_lab),
              plate, north, map_theme)

## Colour limits from robust quantiles. The raw topographic position surface runs
## past 1,000 m at the grid edge, where the 625 m window is truncated, and on a
## full-range ramp that artefact flattens the whole interior to one colour.
panel <- function(r, title, legend, pal = "viridis", dir = 1, q = c(.02, .98)) {
  lim <- unname(quantile(values(r, mat = FALSE), q, na.rm = TRUE))
  ggplot() + geom_spatraster(data = r) +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(option = pal, direction = dir, na.value = "grey88",
                         name = legend, limits = lim, oob = scales::squish) +
    clip_layer + study + labs(title = title, subtitle = sub_utm)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: word-budget
#| echo: true

## The 6,000-word limit is the constraint this file exists to satisfy, so it is
## measured here from the file's own source, at render time, and the render stops if
## the body is over budget. That is deliberately a different measurement from the one
## the post-render stamping script makes: the script counts the rendered document,
## which includes every line of printed code, while this counts body prose only, which
## is what the journal's limit is about. Both numbers are real and they answer
## different questions, so neither replaces the other.
##
## Note for whoever edits this comment: do not write the stamping script's placeholder
## token in any chunk that echoes. The script substitutes on the joined text of any
## paragraph containing it and rewrites that paragraph as a single run, which destroys
## the line breaks of the code listing it appears in.

jae_wordcount <- function(path = "manuscript-short.qmd",
                          from = "# Introduction",
                          to   = "# Conflict of interest") {
  src <- paste(readLines(path, warn = FALSE), collapse = "\n")
  src <- sub("^---.*?\n---\n", "", src)                    # YAML
  src <- gsub("<!--.*?-->", "", src)                       # HTML comments
  src <- gsub("```\\{r[^\n]*\n.*?\n```", "", src)          # code chunks
  ## perl = TRUE on the two line-anchored patterns below is load-bearing, not
  ## decoration. R's default engine lets `.` match a newline and anchors ^ and $
  ## to the whole string, so `gsub("^#+ .*$", "", body)` matches the first
  ## heading and then eats every remaining character of the manuscript. That is
  ## how this guard reported 0 words against a 6,000 limit and passed: a guard
  ## that cannot fail is not a guard. PCRE with (?m) anchors per line and stops
  ## `.` at newlines, which is the behaviour the pattern was always assuming.
  src <- gsub("(?m)^:::.*$", "", src, perl = TRUE)         # div fences
  src <- gsub("`r [^`]*`", "NUM", src)                     # inline code -> one word
  i <- regexpr(from, src, fixed = TRUE)
  j <- regexpr(to,   src, fixed = TRUE)
  if (i < 0) stop("word-budget: start marker not found: ", from)
  body <- if (j > i) substr(src, i, j - 1) else substr(src, i, nchar(src))
  body <- gsub("(?m)^#+ .*$", "", body, perl = TRUE)       # headings are not body prose
  n <- length(strsplit(trimws(body), "\\s+")[[1]])
  ## The failure this guard exists to catch is silence, so refuse a count that
  ## is implausible on its face rather than reporting it.
  if (n < 1000) stop("word-budget: counted ", n, " words, which cannot be right; ",
                     "the stripping regexes have eaten the body again")
  n
}

WC_BODY  <- jae_wordcount()
WC_LIMIT <- 6000L
cat(sprintf("Main text (Introduction to Conclusions, references excluded): %d / %d words\n",
            WC_BODY, WC_LIMIT))
if (WC_BODY > WC_LIMIT)
  stop(sprintf("Over the JAE Original Article limit by %d words.", WC_BODY - WC_LIMIT))
```

# Introduction

Disturbance refugia, defined by @krawchuk2020 as locations "disturbed less severely or less frequently than other areas within the surrounding landscape", organise much of the current thinking about how forests carry biological legacies through disturbance. The empirical base is predominantly a wildfire literature [@krawchuk2020; @littlefield2019]; for insect outbreaks it is thinner, and @krawchuk2020 observe that few studies have explicitly identified refugia from insect outbreaks.

For mountain pine beetle (*Dendroctonus ponderosae* Hopkins), @krawchuk2020 advance three hypotheses: refugia in areas with cooler temperatures that protect trees from water stress, in areas of lower host density "allowing for greater wind disruption of beetle pheromone communication and more vigorous tree growth and chemical defenses", or in areas with fewer large-diameter host trees. All three predict reduced attack on high, cool, sparsely stocked ground, and they are separable only by the mechanism each invokes. We test the second and treat the other two as the competing explanations against which it must be judged.

A structured review of the studies that model bark beetle attack against terrain, reported in full as Appendix S1, makes the evidence countable. Of the studies retained, one enters a wind term, and it is a companion study on this same landscape whose response is conifer regeneration rather than beetle attack (R1). The closest existing test, @cartwright2018, associated refugia with shaded slopes, convergent topographic positions and thinner stands; thin stands are where a wind effect would be expected and also where host is scarce, so separating the two requires an independent host layer (R2). No retained study codes host as the attribute the life history says governs brood production (R3), and none refits one model across extent, grain and response coding to report whether its conclusion survives (R4).

Interpreting any spatial pattern of attack requires the population biology that generates it. Colonisation proceeds by mass attack, a density phenomenon rather than a behaviour. A lodgepole pine (*Pinus contorta* Douglas ex Loudon) resists a single beetle through constitutive resin flow and an induced response that saturates the phloem with terpenes, so overwhelming that defence requires the near-simultaneous arrival of many individuals [@safranyik2006chap1; @clark2010]. Arrival is coordinated chemically: pioneer females oxidise the host monoterpene alpha-pinene to *trans*-verbenol, arriving males release *exo*-brevicomin, and host kairomones synergise both, so colonisation is normally complete within one to two days, until at approximately 60 attacks per square metre of bark *exo*-brevicomin, frontalin and the anti-aggregation pheromone verbenone reverse the signal and redirect arrivals to neighbouring trees [@safranyik2006chap1]. Because that signal is airborne it is in principle susceptible to wind, and that susceptibility is the premise under test.

Host quality sets a second constraint, acting on stem size rather than host abundance. Bark thickness, bark surface area, phloem thickness and sapwood moisture retention all increase with tree diameter and together determine how many beetles a colonised tree produces. @carroll2004bionomics summarise the consequence as a threshold: lodgepole pine of 25 cm diameter or less are on average beetle sinks, in that more beetles attack than emerge, whereas trees above 25 cm are sources. The threshold is stated for individual trees; we apply it to a stand attribute and treat it as an approximate ordering of stand suitability.

Temperature imposes two further constraints, acting on different parts of the life cycle. Development is bounded by heat accumulation, and where accumulation is insufficient, as at high elevation, populations become semivoltine, overwintering twice in cold-susceptible stages and losing the emergence synchrony on which mass attack depends [@safranyik2006chap1; @powell2014]. Overwinter survival is bounded by cold tolerance, which is acquired rather than fixed: glycerol accumulates through autumn, so hardiness peaks from December to February and is incomplete on either side, and tolerance is stage-specific, with lethal ranges of -23 to -29 °C for first instars, -23 to -34 °C for second instars and -29 to -40 °C for third and fourth [@safranyik2006chap1]. The conventionally quoted -40 °C is the cold end of the range for the late instars that normally overwinter, not a threshold for the population, and the same source is explicit that cold arriving before hardening completes does far more damage than the same temperature in midwinter.

Dispersal is bounded thermally before it is bounded by wind. @carroll2004bionomics give a flight envelope of 19 to 41 °C after @mccambridge1971, most beetles flying between 22 and 32 °C, so a cold slope suppresses arrival without any appeal to a pheromone plume. Dispersal is also density-dependent, switching between short-range movement below the canopy and long-range transport above it as population density rises [@powell2014; @johnson2026density], so the spatial signature of attack is itself a function of outbreak phase.

The wind ceiling itself is an inference across species rather than a measurement on this one. @carroll2004bionomics put the maximum wind speed for flight in a large-bodied bark beetle at approximately 2 m per second, citing work on *Dendroctonus pseudotsugae* Hopkins, and the comparative evidence assembled by @jones2019 is consistent but no firmer: in the one wind-tunnel trial on *D. ponderosae* the beetles flew longer at 0, 0.5 and 1 m per second than at 2, which is reduced flight duration rather than arrest.

Testing the hypothesis requires a spatial wind surface, and the available surfaces bound what can be inferred (R5). Gridded products, including the Global Wind Atlas, are produced by driving a mesoscale model from reanalysis, generalising the output to remove local terrain effects, then downscaling it over a digital elevation model and a roughness map [@badger2014; @davis2023]. Elevation is an input to the product rather than a covariate measured independently of it, and the dependence is most severe at small extents, where the driving field is nearly flat. Nor does the atlas report the quantity at issue, an instantaneous below-canopy speed during the July and August flight period, rather than an annual mean at 10 m over open ground. A third confound is specific to refugia work: a cell recorded as unattacked may simply contain no host, and @hadley1994 predicted heavier mortality on hot, dry, south-facing slopes and observed the reverse, because host distribution rather than moisture stress governed where attack succeeded.

We therefore address four questions on a single landscape spanning `r format(round(GRID_RELIEF), big.mark = ",")` m of relief. From R2, does terrain condition beetle-caused mortality once host abundance is accounted for, and where does host distribution cease to explain the pattern? From R3, does that result survive coding host as stem diameter rather than as cover? From R1 and R5, does the component of the wind surface independent of elevation predict reduced attack where host is present? And from R4, how far does that answer depend on decisions the data do not fix: the extent of the study area, the grain of the cells, and whether damage is coded as binary or as the ordinal severity class the survey records?

# Materials and methods

## Study area

The Darkwoods Conservation Area lies in the South Selkirk Mountains of southeastern British Columbia. The terrain grid spans 16 by 17.5 km and `r format(round(GRID_RELIEF), big.mark = ",")` m of relief, from valley bottom to alpine; the modelled area is a subset, because cells carrying no inventory basal area cannot enter a model conditioning on stand structure, and @tbl-relief reports its extent. The range crosses the full biogeoclimatic sequence of the southern interior wet belt, from the dry warm Interior Cedar-Hemlock subzones to the Engelmann Spruce-Subalpine Fir zone and its parkland variant [@ketcheson1991; @braumandl2005], and lodgepole pine occupies the middle of that sequence. Terrain surfaces and the site description are inherited from a companion analysis on the same ground [@murphy2026], in which disturbance was a predictor; here it is the response.

## Beetle-caused mortality

```{r}
#| label: read-response
#| echo: true

aos_box <- ext(project(as.polygons(ext(G), crs = crs(G)), "EPSG:3005"))
aos <- vect(here("02.inputs/aos/pest_infestation_poly.gdb"),
            layer = "pest_infestation_poly", extent = aos_box)
mpb <- project(aos[aos$PEST_SPECIES_CODE == "IBM", ], crs(G))   # IBM = mountain pine beetle
m   <- mpb[mpb$CAPTURE_YEAR %in% OUTBREAK, ]

## BC severity classes are ordinal: trace, light, moderate, severe, very severe
sev_rank <- c(T = 1, L = 2, M = 3, S = 4, V = 5)
m$sev <- unname(sev_rank[m$PEST_SEVERITY_CODE]); m$sev[is.na(m$sev)] <- 0

severity  <- rasterize(m, G, field = "sev", fun = "max", background = 0)

c(polygons = nrow(m), years = length(unique(m$CAPTURE_YEAR)),
  hectares = round(sum(m$AREA_HA)))
```

The response is the British Columbia Aerial Overview Survey, the operational provincial record of forest health, in which observers sketch-map damage annually from aircraft and label each polygon by year, causal agent, severity class and host species. We take polygons coded `IBM`, mountain pine beetle, for the outbreak window 1999 to 2015, and rasterise the maximum severity class reached by each cell.

The survey was preferred to a spectral classification for a specific reason. Red attack has been mapped from Landsat with improving accuracy [@white2005; @meddens2013; @ye2021], but every such product is a model whose errors are spatially structured and not independent of terrain, because illumination, shadow and view angle vary with slope and aspect. For a question about terrain, a response drawn from a terrain-sensitive classifier risks recovering the classifier's own terrain sensitivity. Sketch-mapping has cruder errors, but they are observer errors rather than errors generated by the predictors under test. Twenty-eight field plots established in 2020 recorded the basal area of pine killed, spanning 0.6 to 47.4 m2/ha, and anchor the severity scale [@murphy2026]; their coordinates were not recoverable, so no validation of polygon placement is claimed.

```{r}
#| label: fig-site
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 7.1
#| fig-height: 6.8
#| fig-cap: "The study area and the three spatial inputs. (a) Location within British Columbia; the marker is a 22 km symbol, not the footprint. (b) The elevation surface, which is the analysis grid. (c) Global Wind Atlas mean speed at 10 m; the shaded southern band lies outside the wind product's extent. (d) Beetle-caused mortality from the Aerial Overview Survey, 1999 to 2015, as the maximum severity class in any year. The outlined rectangle in (b) to (d) is the 2 by 4 km clip of @sec-extent. Each panel's graticule, axis ticks and stated coordinate reference system are the same; the system is named beneath the panel title and ticks are in kilometres."

## The wind raster begins 715 m north of the grid's southern edge, so resampling onto G
## turns that strip into NA cells and na.value draws it grey. Left transparent it reads
## as a rendering fault rather than as missing data.
Wind_r <- resample(rast(dpath("terrain_environment", "Wind.utm.tif")), G)

prov <- st_transform(ne_states(country = c("Canada","United States of America"),
                               returnclass = "sf"), 3005)
site <- st_transform(st_centroid(grid_sf), 3005)
lab  <- transform(as.data.frame(st_coordinates(site)), lab = "Darkwoods\nstudy area")
## BC is framed to the analysis grid's aspect ratio so the two rows of the figure are
## the same height and no band of white opens between them.
b0 <- st_bbox(prov[prov$name == "British Columbia", ]); tgt <- unname(gw/gh)
w0 <- unname(b0["xmax"]-b0["xmin"]); h0 <- unname(b0["ymax"]-b0["ymin"])
cx <- unname(b0["xmax"]+b0["xmin"])/2; cy <- unname(b0["ymax"]+b0["ymin"])/2
if (w0/h0 > tgt) h0 <- w0/tgt else w0 <- h0*tgt
pd <- .04*w0
bb <- c(xmin = cx-w0/2-pd, xmax = cx+w0/2+pd, ymin = cy-h0/2-pd, ymax = cy+h0/2+pd)

p_a <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = prov[prov$name != "British Columbia", ], fill = "grey93",
          colour = "grey65", linewidth = .2) +
  geom_sf(data = prov[prov$name == "British Columbia", ], fill = "grey82",
          colour = "grey30", linewidth = .4) +
  geom_sf(data = st_buffer(site, 22000), fill = "#C0392B", colour = "grey15",
          linewidth = .3) +
  geom_label_repel(data = lab, aes(X, Y, label = lab), size = 2.1, lineheight = .95,
                   colour = "grey10", nudge_x = -330000, nudge_y = 300000,
                   segment.colour = "grey25", segment.size = .3, min.segment.length = 0,
                   box.padding = .4, seed = 1, fill = "white", alpha = .9,
                   label.size = 0, label.padding = unit(.7, "mm")) +
  annotate("text", x = bb["xmin"] + .34*(bb["xmax"]-bb["xmin"]),
           y = bb["ymin"] + .70*(bb["ymax"]-bb["ymin"]), label = "British\nColumbia",
           size = 2.3, colour = "grey30", fontface = "italic", lineheight = .95) +
  coord_sf(crs = 3005, xlim = bb[c("xmin","xmax")], ylim = bb[c("ymin","ymax")],
           datum = st_crs(3005), expand = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = scales::breaks_pretty(3), labels = km_lab) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = scales::breaks_pretty(3), labels = km_lab) +
  north + map_theme +
  labs(title = "(a) Location", subtitle = sub_alb)

p_b <- ggplot() + geom_spatraster(data = G) +
  scale_fill_hypso_c(palette = "dem_screen", na.value = "transparent",
                     name = "Elevation\n(m)") +
  clip_layer + study + labs(title = "(b) Elevation, the analysis grid", subtitle = sub_utm)

p_c <- ggplot() + geom_spatraster(data = Wind_r) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "mako", direction = -1, na.value = "grey88",
                       name = "Wind speed\n(m s⁻¹)") +
  clip_layer + study +
  labs(title = "(c) Global Wind Atlas mean speed at 10 m", subtitle = sub_utm)

sev_f <- as.factor(severity)
levels(sev_f) <- data.frame(ID = 0:5, class = c("none","trace","light","moderate",
                                                "severe","very severe"))
p_d <- ggplot() + geom_spatraster(data = sev_f) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(none = "grey92", trace = "#FEE0B6", light = "#FDB863",
                    moderate = "#E08214", severe = "#B35806", `very severe` = "#7F3B08"),
                    na.value = "transparent", name = "Severity\nclass",
                    na.translate = FALSE) +
  clip_layer + study +
  labs(title = "(d) Beetle-caused mortality, 1999 to 2015", subtitle = sub_utm)

fig_site <- (p_a | p_b) / (p_c | p_d)
fig_site
ggsave("../03.outputs/PNG/fig-site-maps.png", fig_site,
       width = 180, height = 172, units = "mm", dpi = 500, bg = "white")
```

## Red-stage classification

The survey resolves damage at the scale an observer can sketch from an aircraft, and the refugia question is about wind and terrain acting at tens of metres, so we classified red-stage attack annually from Landsat across the whole grid to see whether a finer response layer would support the test the polygons cannot. The result is reported here rather than in Results because it decides which response layer the paper uses. Every stage runs in Google Earth Engine through `rgee`, gated on the exported rasters.

```{r}
#| label: ee-pipeline-setup
#| echo: true

RED_DIR   <- here("02.inputs/beetle-classification/red-stage")
BASE_YEAR <- 2003          # differencing baseline, see below
CLASS_YRS <- 2005:2014
dec_files <- file.path(RED_DIR, sprintf("dec_%d.tif", CLASS_YRS))

## Sensor supplying each year, taken from Landsat scene metadata rather than
## from the parent study's Table 2, which lists Landsat 5 for a 2013 acquisition.
## Landsat 5 stopped acquiring in November 2011 and Landsat 8 did not begin until
## 2013, so 2012 is the one year only Landsat 7 covers. The parent study omitted
## 2012 for that reason and not for cloud: six Landsat 7 scenes met its own
## selection rule of under 20 per cent cloud between 1 June and 30 August, the
## cleanest at 1 per cent. Landsat 7 has flown scan-line-corrector-off since May
## 2003, so that year alone carries striping. Inventory in
## 02.inputs/beetle-classification/landsat-scene-inventory.csv.
SENSOR <- c(`2003`="LT05",`2005`="LT05",`2006`="LT05",`2007`="LT05",`2008`="LT05",
            `2009`="LT05",`2010`="LT05",`2011`="LT05",`2012`="LE07",
            `2013`="LC08",`2014`="LC08")
COLL   <- c(LT05="LANDSAT/LT05/C02/T1_L2", LE07="LANDSAT/LE07/C02/T1_L2",
            LC08="LANDSAT/LC08/C02/T1_L2")
SB     <- c("BLUE","GREEN","RED","NIR","SWIR1","SWIR2")
BANDS  <- c(SB, "NDMI", "dNDMI")
```

```{r}
#| label: ee-pipeline-functions
#| echo: true

## Stage 1, imagery. Collection 2 Level-2 surface reflectance, scaled by the
## published factors, with cloud, cloud shadow, cirrus and snow masked from
## QA_PIXEL bits 1 to 5. Thematic Mapper and Enhanced Thematic Mapper carry the
## reflective bands as SR_B1-5 and SR_B7; the Operational Land Imager shifts them
## to SR_B2-7 because it adds a coastal aerosol band. Both are renamed to common
## names so nothing downstream has to know which sensor it is reading.
ee_prep <- function(sensor) {
  bn <- if (sensor == "LC08") paste0("SR_B", 2:7) else paste0("SR_B", c(1:5, 7))
  rgee::ee_utils_pyfunc(function(im) {
    qa   <- im$select("QA_PIXEL")
    keep <- qa$bitwiseAnd(2L)$eq(0)$And(qa$bitwiseAnd(4L)$eq(0))$
      And(qa$bitwiseAnd(8L)$eq(0))$And(qa$bitwiseAnd(16L)$eq(0))$
      And(qa$bitwiseAnd(32L)$eq(0))
    im$select(bn, SB)$multiply(0.0000275)$add(-0.2)$updateMask(keep)$
      copyProperties(im, list("SUN_ELEVATION","SUN_AZIMUTH","system:time_start"))
  })
}

ee_year <- function(y, AOI) {
  s <- SENSOR[[as.character(y)]]
  ee$ImageCollection(COLL[[s]])$filterBounds(AOI)$
    filterDate(sprintf("%d-06-01", y), sprintf("%d-08-31", y))$
    filter(ee$Filter$lt("CLOUD_COVER", 60))$map(ee_prep(s))
}

## Stage 2, terrain correction. Mandatory here and not at the 7.78 km2 extent the
## parent study worked at. Across 1,776 m of relief, illumination varies enough
## with slope and aspect to put a terrain signal into reflectance, and this study
## tests terrain effects, so an uncorrected artefact would be indistinguishable
## from the result. SCS+C after Soenen et al. 2005: the C term is the ratio of
## intercept to slope in a regression of reflectance on the illumination term,
## fitted per band per scene. Where a scene is wholly masked over the grid the
## regression returns null; C is then set very large, which drives the correction
## factor to one, so a scene with nothing to fit is passed through unchanged
## rather than destroyed.
ee_illum <- function(im, slope, asp) {
  sz <- ee$Image$constant(90)$subtract(ee$Number(im$get("SUN_ELEVATION")))$multiply(pi/180)
  sa <- ee$Image$constant(ee$Number(im$get("SUN_AZIMUTH")))$multiply(pi/180)
  slope$cos()$multiply(sz$cos())$
    add(slope$sin()$multiply(sz$sin())$multiply(sa$subtract(asp)$cos()))$rename("cos_i")
}

ee_scs_c <- function(im, slope, asp, AOI) {
  ci <- ee_illum(im, slope, asp)
  sz <- ee$Image$constant(90)$subtract(ee$Number(im$get("SUN_ELEVATION")))$multiply(pi/180)
  n0 <- slope$cos()$multiply(sz$cos())
  one <- function(b) {
    f  <- ci$addBands(im$select(b))$reduceRegion(ee$Reducer$linearFit(), AOI, 90,
                                                 maxPixels = 1e9, bestEffort = TRUE)
    sc <- ee$Number(ee$Algorithms$If(f$get("scale"),  f$get("scale"),  0))
    of <- ee$Number(ee$Algorithms$If(f$get("offset"), f$get("offset"), 0))
    C  <- ee$Number(ee$Algorithms$If(sc$abs()$gt(1e-8), of$divide(sc), 1e6))$max(0)$min(1e6)
    im$select(b)$multiply(n0$add(C))$divide(ci$add(C))$rename(b)
  }
  bs <- one(SB[1]); for (b in SB[-1]) bs <- bs$addBands(one(b))
  bs$copyProperties(im, list("SUN_ELEVATION","SUN_AZIMUTH","system:time_start"))
}

## Stage 3, index and differencing. NDMI is (NIR - SWIR1) / (NIR + SWIR1) and each
## annual composite is differenced against the pre-outbreak baseline. The baseline
## is 2003, not the 2005 the parent study's text names twice. Its own Table 2
## labels 2003 pre-outbreak and 2005 early-outbreak, and its 2005 raster carries
## 534 cells coded red attack, 9.73 per cent of the cells it maps. A scene
## differenced against itself is zero everywhere, so 2005 cannot be its own
## baseline. See 02.inputs/beetle-classification/02-parent-raster-audit.R.
ee_stack <- function(y, BASE, slope, asp, AOI) {
  m  <- ee_year(y, AOI)$map(rgee::ee_utils_pyfunc(
          function(im) ee$Image(ee_scs_c(im, slope, asp, AOI))))$median()
  nd <- m$normalizedDifference(c("NIR","SWIR1"))$rename("NDMI")
  m$addBands(nd)$addBands(nd$subtract(BASE)$rename("dNDMI"))
}
```

The classifier is trained on the aerial overview survey itself, because an earlier 310-row spectral sample derives from a single uncorrected 2020 Landsat 8 scene and would be mapping attack from 2005 to 2014, eight of those years from a different satellite. Training on the survey keeps labels and imagery in the same year and the same radiometry.

```{r}
#| label: ee-classify
#| echo: true

SAMP_FILE <- file.path(RED_DIR, "training-sample.csv")

## Stage 4, labels. Positives are cells the survey mapped at moderate severity or
## worse in that year, negatives cells it mapped as undamaged, 250 of each per
## year with a quarter held out. 2014 takes the pooled model because the survey
## records no cell above trace over this grid that year.
##
## The sample is written to disk and the classifier is then trained from the
## table rather than from the sampling graph. That is not tidiness. An Earth
## Engine classifier carries its training computation into every image it is
## later applied to, so classifying an annual composite from a classifier trained
## directly on nine years of sampled composites re-runs all of it and the
## download fails with a 400. Trained from stored numbers, the same download
## succeeds.
if (!file.exists(SAMP_FILE)) {
  library(rgee); ee_Initialize(project = "murphys-deforisk", quiet = TRUE)
  dir.create(RED_DIR, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  AOI   <- ee$Geometry$Rectangle(c(-116.7861, 49.0884, -116.5649, 49.2460))
  DEM   <- ee$Image("USGS/SRTMGL1_003")
  slope <- ee$Terrain$slope(DEM)$multiply(pi/180)
  asp   <- ee$Terrain$aspect(DEM)$multiply(pi/180)
  BASE  <- ee_year(BASE_YEAR, AOI)$map(rgee::ee_utils_pyfunc(
             function(im) ee$Image(ee_scs_c(im, slope, asp, AOI))))$median()$
             normalizedDifference(c("NIR","SWIR1"))$rename("NDMI")

  set.seed(42); parts <- list()
  for (y in 2005:2013) {
    ry <- rasterize(m[m$CAPTURE_YEAR == y, ], G, field = "sev",
                    fun = "max", background = 0)
    if (global(ry >= 3, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]] < 30) next
    pick <- function(mk, lab) {
      p <- spatSample(mk, 250, "random", na.rm = TRUE, xy = TRUE, values = FALSE)
      data.frame(x = p[,1], y = p[,2], lab = lab,
                 elev = extract(G, p[,1:2])[,1], yr = y)
    }
    d <- rbind(pick(ifel(ry >= 3, 1, NA), 1L), pick(ifel(ry == 0, 1, NA), 0L))
    d <- d[!is.na(d$elev), ]
    d$split <- as.integer(runif(nrow(d)) < 0.25)
    pts <- sf::st_transform(sf::st_as_sf(d, coords = c("x","y"), crs = crs(G)), 4326)
    parts[[length(parts) + 1]] <- ee_stack(y, BASE, slope, asp, AOI)$sampleRegions(
      collection = sf_as_ee(pts), properties = list("lab","elev","yr","split"),
      scale = 30, tileScale = 4, geometries = TRUE)
  }
  got <- ee_as_sf(ee$FeatureCollection(parts)$flatten(), quiet = TRUE)
  xy  <- sf::st_coordinates(got)
  write.csv(cbind(sf::st_drop_geometry(got), lon = xy[,1], lat = xy[,2]),
            SAMP_FILE, row.names = FALSE)
}
samp <- read.csv(SAMP_FILE)
stopifnot(all(c(BANDS, "lab", "elev", "yr", "split", "lon", "lat") %in% names(samp)))

## Stage 4b, the classifier. Fitted here rather than by ee$Classifier$libsvm,
## for a mechanical reason. An Earth Engine classifier carries its training
## features into every request that uses it, so each annual download embedded the
## whole labelled table and returned HTTP 400; the same eight-band composite
## downloads without complaint on its own. A linear kernel is a plane, so the
## fitted model transfers exactly as a band expression and Earth Engine is left
## doing arithmetic. The check below is that transfer, and it holds to machine
## precision. Predictors are standardised on the training rows only.
SVM_TR <- samp[samp$split == 0, ]; SVM_TE <- samp[samp$split == 1, ]
SVM_MU <- sapply(SVM_TR[BANDS], mean); SVM_SD <- sapply(SVM_TR[BANDS], sd)
zscore <- function(d) as.matrix(sweep(sweep(d[BANDS], 2, SVM_MU, "-"), 2, SVM_SD, "/"))
set.seed(1)
SVM_FIT <- kernlab::ksvm(zscore(SVM_TR), factor(SVM_TR$lab), type = "C-svc",
                         kernel = "vanilladot", C = 1, scaled = FALSE)
SVM_W <- colSums(kernlab::coef(SVM_FIT)[[1]] * kernlab::xmatrix(SVM_FIT)[[1]])
SVM_B <- -SVM_FIT@b
stopifnot(identical(
  as.integer(as.vector(zscore(SVM_TE) %*% SVM_W + SVM_B) > 0),
  as.integer(as.character(predict(SVM_FIT, zscore(SVM_TE))))))

## Collapsed into raw reflectance units, which is the form Earth Engine applies.
SVM_A <- SVM_W / SVM_SD
SVM_C <- SVM_B - sum(SVM_W * SVM_MU / SVM_SD)
stopifnot(max(abs((as.matrix(SVM_TE[BANDS]) %*% SVM_A + SVM_C) -
                  (zscore(SVM_TE) %*% SVM_W + SVM_B))) < 1e-8)

## Stage 5, validation. Computed here from the held-out quarter, so the agreement
## table below and the exported rasters come from one fitted object.
SVM_TE$pred <- as.integer(as.vector(as.matrix(SVM_TE[BANDS]) %*% SVM_A + SVM_C) > 0)

if (!all(file.exists(dec_files))) {
  library(rgee); ee_Initialize(project = "murphys-deforisk", quiet = TRUE)
  AOI   <- ee$Geometry$Rectangle(c(-116.7861, 49.0884, -116.5649, 49.2460))
  DEM   <- ee$Image("USGS/SRTMGL1_003")
  slope <- ee$Terrain$slope(DEM)$multiply(pi/180)
  asp   <- ee$Terrain$aspect(DEM)$multiply(pi/180)
  BASE  <- ee_year(BASE_YEAR, AOI)$map(rgee::ee_utils_pyfunc(
             function(im) ee$Image(ee_scs_c(im, slope, asp, AOI))))$median()$
             normalizedDifference(c("NIR","SWIR1"))$rename("NDMI")

  ## Stage 6, export. The decision plane is applied band by band, thresholded at
  ## zero, classified at the 30 m native grid, then resampled onto the analysis
  ## grid by nearest neighbour, which is the correct rule for a class raster and
  ## makes the alignment exact rather than nearly so.
  gbox <- ee$Geometry$Rectangle(c(xmin(G), ymin(G), xmax(G), ymax(G)),
                                proj = "EPSG:32611", geodesic = FALSE)
  for (y in CLASS_YRS) {
    st <- ee_stack(y, BASE, slope, asp, AOI)
    d  <- ee$Image$constant(SVM_C)
    for (bn in BANDS) d <- d$add(st$select(bn)$multiply(unname(SVM_A[bn])))
    ## The continuous decision value is exported, not a thresholded map, so the
    ## threshold stays a visible choice made below rather than one baked into a
    ## download. Scaled by 1,000 and offset by 10,000 because a GeoTIFF written
    ## from an integer image takes zero as its nodata value: exporting a signed
    ## surface directly would silently delete every cell sitting on the decision
    ## boundary, and exporting a 0/1 map deleted every unattacked cell outright
    ## on the first attempt, returning 100 per cent attacked in all ten years.
    u <- d$multiply(1000)$add(10000)$round()$toInt16()$rename("dec")$
      getDownloadURL(list(name = sprintf("dec_%d", y), crs = "EPSG:32611",
                          scale = 30, region = gbox, format = "GEO_TIFF"))
    tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".tif"); download.file(u, tmp, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
    ## Kept in the scaled integer form Earth Engine sent, deflated, because the
    ## same surface as 32-bit float is 2.2 MB a year and this is 0.2 MB. The
    ## offset is removed at read time below, not here.
    writeRaster(resample(rast(tmp), G, method = "bilinear"),
                file.path(RED_DIR, sprintf("dec_%d.tif", y)),
                overwrite = TRUE, datatype = "INT2S",
                gdal = c("COMPRESS=DEFLATE", "PREDICTOR=2"))
  }
}

dec <- (rast(dec_files) - 10000) / 1000     # undo the export scaling and offset
names(dec) <- CLASS_YRS

## The model's own threshold is zero, which is what a balanced training sample
## implies. It is the wrong prior for this landscape. Training drew 250 attacked
## and 250 unattacked cells per year, so the implied prevalence is one half,
## while the survey maps attack on a few per cent of the grid. Thresholded at
## zero the classification calls a third to two thirds of the landscape attacked.
## Both maps are therefore carried: the model's own, and one whose threshold is
## calibrated per year so the classified area matches the area the survey mapped.
SURV_AREA <- sapply(CLASS_YRS, function(y) {
  ry <- rasterize(m[m$CAPTURE_YEAR == y, ], G, field = "sev", fun = "max", background = 0)
  global(ry >= 3, "mean", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]]
})
names(SURV_AREA) <- CLASS_YRS
RAW_AREA <- sapply(CLASS_YRS, function(y)
  global(dec[[as.character(y)]] > 0, "mean", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]])
names(RAW_AREA) <- CLASS_YRS

red <- rast(lapply(CLASS_YRS, function(y) {
  d <- dec[[as.character(y)]]
  thr <- if (SURV_AREA[[as.character(y)]] > 0)
    global(d, function(v, ...) quantile(v, 1 - SURV_AREA[[as.character(y)]], na.rm = TRUE))[[1]]
    else Inf
  d > thr
}))
names(red) <- CLASS_YRS
## A classification that is entirely one class, or entirely masked, is a
## pipeline failure rather than a result, and must not reach the prose.
stopifnot(nlyr(red) == length(CLASS_YRS),
          all(dim(red)[1:2] == dim(G)[1:2]),
          isTRUE(all.equal(as.vector(ext(red)), as.vector(ext(G)), tolerance = 1e-6)),
          all(RAW_AREA > 0.001), all(RAW_AREA < 0.999),
          all(global(!is.na(red), "mean")[[1]] > 0.5))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-redstage
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Agreement between the Landsat red-stage classification and the aerial overview survey, by 300 m elevation band. The held-out quarter of the labelled sample, pooled over 2005 to 2013. This is agreement with the survey, not accuracy against ground truth: the survey is also the training source, and no independent reference exists at this extent."

v <- SVM_TE
v$classification <- v$pred
v$band <- cut(v$elev, seq(500, 2400, by = 300), dig.lab = 5)

kap <- function(o, p) {
  cm <- table(factor(o, 0:1), factor(p, 0:1))
  oa <- sum(diag(cm)) / sum(cm)
  pe <- sum(rowSums(cm) * colSums(cm)) / sum(cm)^2
  c(OA = oa, kappa = (oa - pe) / (1 - pe))
}
POOLED <- kap(v$lab, v$classification)

RED_TBL <- do.call(rbind, lapply(levels(v$band), function(b) {
  s <- v[!is.na(v$band) & v$band == b, ]
  if (nrow(s) < 10)
    return(data.frame(Band = b, n = nrow(s), Attacked = sum(s$lab == 1),
                      Agreement = NA_real_, Kappa = NA_real_,
                      Note = "too few reference points, uncertain"))
  k <- kap(s$lab, s$classification)
  data.frame(Band = b, n = nrow(s), Attacked = sum(s$lab == 1),
             Agreement = round(k["OA"], 3), Kappa = round(k["kappa"], 3), Note = "")
}))
kable(RED_TBL, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("Elevation band (m)", "n", "Attacked", "Agreement", "Kappa", ""))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-redstage-area
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Where the Landsat classification and the aerial overview survey disagree, by year. Survey area is the share of the grid the survey mapped at moderate severity or worse. Model area is what the classifier calls attacked at its own threshold of zero. Hit rate is the share of calibrated classified cells that fall inside a survey polygon, and lift is that rate divided by the survey's own prevalence, so 1.00 is chance."

RED_CMP <- do.call(rbind, lapply(CLASS_YRS, function(y) {
  yc <- as.character(y)
  ry <- rasterize(m[m$CAPTURE_YEAR == y, ], G, field = "sev", fun = "max", background = 0)
  S  <- ry >= 3
  p  <- SURV_AREA[[yc]]
  if (p == 0) return(data.frame(Year = y, Survey = 0, Model = round(100*RAW_AREA[[yc]], 1),
                                Hit = NA_real_, Lift = NA_real_))
  hits <- global(S & red[[yc]], "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]]
  nC   <- global(red[[yc]], "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]]
  data.frame(Year = y, Survey = round(100*p, 3), Model = round(100*RAW_AREA[[yc]], 1),
             Hit = round(100*hits/nC, 2), Lift = round((hits/nC)/p, 2))
}))
kable(RED_CMP, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("Year", "Survey area (%)", "Model area (%)",
                    "Hit rate (%)", "Lift"))
```

The classification does not replace the survey, and the reason is not a marginal shortfall in accuracy. Pooled over the held-out quarter it agrees with the survey on `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * POOLED["OA"])` per cent of cells, kappa `r sprintf("%.2f", POOLED["kappa"])`, but @tbl-redstage-area shows that figure is flattered by the sampling. Training took 250 attacked and 250 unattacked cells per year, an implied prevalence of one half against a true `r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * min(SURV_AREA[SURV_AREA > 0]))` to `r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * max(SURV_AREA))` per cent, so at its own threshold the classifier calls `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * min(RAW_AREA))` to `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * max(RAW_AREA))` per cent of the landscape attacked. Calibrating the threshold each year so that classified area equals surveyed area, it lands on `r sprintf("%.1f", min(RED_CMP$Hit, na.rm = TRUE))` to `r sprintf("%.1f", max(RED_CMP$Hit, na.rm = TRUE))` per cent of the cells the survey mapped, a lift of `r sprintf("%.2f", min(RED_CMP$Lift, na.rm = TRUE))` to `r sprintf("%.2f", max(RED_CMP$Lift, na.rm = TRUE))` against a chance value of 1.00, and `r sum(RED_CMP$Lift == 0, na.rm = TRUE)` of `r sum(!is.na(RED_CMP$Lift))` years share no cells with the survey at all. The clearest diagnostic is 2012, the only year covered by Landsat 7 alone, whose scan line corrector has been broken since May 2003: it is the year the classifier calls most attacked, at `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * RAW_AREA[["2012"]])` per cent, and the year the survey maps least, at `r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * SURV_AREA[["2012"]])` per cent. The classifier is reading striping as change, and an instrument genuinely resolving attack the surveyor missed would still overlap the attack the surveyor found.

We therefore keep the survey as the response and report the classification as a comparison layer, which also means the timing analysis a per-cell year of first detection would allow is unavailable.

## Host attributes

```{r}
#| label: read-host
#| echo: true

vri <- project(vect(here("02.inputs/vri/vri_darkwoods.geojson")), crs(G))
vd  <- as.data.frame(vri)
num <- function(x) suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x))

## VRI records up to three species per polygon with percentage cover
accumulate <- function(pattern) {
  out <- rep(0, nrow(vd))
  for (i in 1:3) {
    cd <- vd[[paste0("SPECIES_CD_", i)]]
    pc <- num(vd[[paste0("SPECIES_PCT_", i)]]); pc[is.na(pc)] <- 0
    out <- out + ifelse(!is.na(cd) & grepl(pattern, cd), pc, 0)
  }
  out
}
vri$PinePct <- accumulate("^PL")               # lodgepole, the primary host
vri$Basal   <- num(vd$BASAL_AREA)

## Quadratic mean diameter of stems 12.5 cm and over. Carried because stem size,
## not cover, is what decides whether a stand produces more beetles than it
## consumes: below about 25 cm a lodgepole stand is a sink, above it a source
## [@carroll2004bionomics]. Cover and basal area cannot express that.
vri$QMD <- num(vd$QUAD_DIAM_125)

host <- rast(lapply(c("PinePct","Basal","QMD"), function(f) rasterize(vri, G, field = f)))
names(host) <- c("PinePct","Basal","QMD")
c(vri_polygons = nrow(vri), with_lodgepole = sum(vri$PinePct > 0),
  with_diameter = sum(!is.na(vri$QMD)))
```

Host abundance comes from the provincial Vegetation Resources Inventory, layer `VEG_COMP_LYR_R1_POLY`. We accumulate the percentage cover of lodgepole pine across the three species slots each polygon records, and carry stand basal area and quadratic mean diameter, the latter recorded for stems 12.5 cm and over. Cover and basal area describe how much host is present; neither describes whether that host can produce beetles, which is the gap R3 identifies. Diameter is recorded for `r format(sum(!is.na(vri$QMD)), big.mark=",")` of the `r format(nrow(vri), big.mark=",")` polygons, covering the analysis frame almost exactly.

The inventory's vintage matters. These polygons carry an interpretation date of August 2014, so composition comes from photography flown in the fourteenth year of a seventeen-year outbreak. A stand whose pine was killed early was interpreted after the fact, so host is under-recorded exactly where attack was heaviest and earliest, which is a candidate explanation for the reversal of the lodgepole coefficient at the severe threshold reported below. It does not touch the presence-absence distinction the layer is mainly used for.

```{r}
#| label: fig-host
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 7.1
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-cap: "The forest inventory host layers, rasterised onto the analysis grid. (a) Lodgepole pine cover, accumulated across the three species slots each polygon records. (b) Stand basal area, which defines the analysis frame: cells with no recorded basal area are dropped. Unshaded ground is unmapped or non-productive. Projection and scale as in @fig-site."

fig_host <-
  (ggplot() + geom_spatraster(data = host$PinePct) +
     scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "viridis", direction = -1, na.value = "grey88",
                          name = "Lodgepole\ncover (%)") +
     clip_layer + study + labs(title = "(a) Lodgepole pine cover", subtitle = sub_utm)) |
  (ggplot() + geom_spatraster(data = host$Basal) +
     scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "plasma", direction = -1, na.value = "grey88",
                          name = "Basal area\n(m² ha⁻¹)") +
     clip_layer + study + labs(title = "(b) Stand basal area", subtitle = sub_utm))
fig_host
ggsave("../03.outputs/PNG/fig-host-maps.png", fig_host,
       width = 180, height = 96, units = "mm", dpi = 500, bg = "white")
```

## Terrain and wind

```{r}
#| label: read-terrain
#| echo: true

to_grid <- function(f) {
  r <- rast(dpath("terrain_environment", f))
  b <- project(as.polygons(ext(G), crs = crs(G)), crs(r))
  project(crop(r, b, snap = "out"), G, method = "bilinear")
}
terr <- rast(list(Elevation = G,               Slope = to_grid("Slope.utm.tif"),
                  TWI       = to_grid("TWI.utm.tif"),
                  RIX       = to_grid("Rutm.tif"),
                  Wind      = to_grid("Wind.utm.tif")))
names(terr) <- c("Elevation","Slope","TWI","RIX","Wind")

## Topographic position: mean deviation from a surrounding annulus.
tpi <- function(r, w) {
  k <- matrix(1, w, w); k[ceiling(w/2), ceiling(w/2)] <- 0
  r - focal(r, k / sum(k), fun = sum, na.policy = "omit", na.rm = TRUE)
}
terr$TPI600 <- tpi(G, 25)     # ~625 m neighbourhood
```

```{r}
#| label: aspect-terms
#| echo: true

## Two surfaces built from aspect, which the inherited set lacks entirely.
## Both are computed directly from the elevation model rather than draped over
## it, which is why @tbl-orthogonality can show them independent of elevation.
d2r <- pi / 180
asp  <- rast(dpath("terrain_environment", "Aspect.utm.tif"))
slp  <- rast(dpath("terrain_environment", "Slope.utm.tif"))
stopifnot(identical(dim(asp), dim(G)), identical(as.vector(ext(asp)), as.vector(ext(G))))

## Heat load after McCune and Keon, aspect folded about the SW-NE axis so that
## southwest is hottest. Flat cells carry a -1 sentinel; the sin(slope) factor
## nulls the aspect term there, so the substitution below is inert.
asp[asp < 0] <- 225
fold <- abs(180 - abs(asp - 225))
LAT  <- mean(crds(project(as.polygons(ext(G), crs = crs(G)), "EPSG:4326"))[, 2])
terr$HLI <- 0.339 + 0.808 * cos(LAT*d2r) * cos(slp*d2r) -
            0.196 * sin(LAT*d2r) * sin(slp*d2r) -
            0.482 * cos(fold*d2r) * sin(slp*d2r)

## Winstral shelter index: the maximum upwind slope angle within SEARCH metres
## along a bearing. Positive means terrain rises upwind, so the cell is
## sheltered; negative means it is exposed. The Global Wind Atlas gives speed
## but no direction, so rather than assume a prevailing bearing we compute all
## eight and average, giving an omnidirectional shelter index.
SEARCH <- 500
shift_mat <- function(m, dr, dc) {
  nr <- nrow(m); nc <- ncol(m); out <- matrix(NA_real_, nr, nc)
  ri <- seq_len(nr); ci <- seq_len(nc); sr <- ri + dr; sc <- ci + dc
  vr <- sr >= 1 & sr <= nr; vc <- sc >= 1 & sc <= nc
  out[ri[vr], ci[vc]] <- m[sr[vr], sc[vc]]
  out
}
zm <- as.matrix(G, wide = TRUE); rstep <- res(G)[1]
sx_dir <- function(az) {
  th <- az * d2r; best <- matrix(-Inf, nrow(zm), ncol(zm))
  for (k in 1:floor(SEARCH / rstep)) {
    dc <- round(k * sin(th)); dr <- round(-k * cos(th))
    if (dc == 0 && dr == 0) next
    best <- pmax(best, atan((shift_mat(zm, dr, dc) - zm) / (k * rstep)) / d2r, na.rm = TRUE)
  }
  best[!is.finite(best)] <- NA_real_
  best
}
sx <- rast(lapply(seq(0, 315, by = 45), function(a) {
  r <- G; values(r) <- as.vector(t(sx_dir(a))); r }))
terr$SxMean <- app(sx, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Terrain surfaces are inherited unchanged from @murphy2026, derived from the 1 m Natural Resources Canada High Resolution Digital Elevation Model [@nrcan2017], smoothed, depression-filled by the algorithm of @wang2006 and aggregated to 25 m, with compound indices following @beers1973 and @parker1982. We add a topographic position index at a 625 m neighbourhood, which the inherited set lacked, and two aspect terms, because that set carries nothing distinguishing a warm slope from a cold one at the same elevation and the confound this paper cannot resolve is between wind exposure and cold. Heat load follows @mccune2002, aspect folded about the southwest to northeast axis so that southwest is hottest. The shelter index follows @winstral2002, the maximum upwind slope angle within 500 m along a bearing, averaged over all eight cardinal and intercardinal bearings because the atlas supplies no direction.

The decisive property of both is how they are built. They are derived from the elevation model by trigonometry rather than draped over it by downscaling, and @tbl-orthogonality shows the consequence: their variance is essentially unrelated to elevation, where the wind product's is largely elevation. A terrain-derived predictor is not automatically an elevation transform; the distinction is in the construction. Ambient wind is Global Wind Atlas mean speed at 10 m above ground level [@globalwindatlas], built by the downscaling chain described in the Introduction.

## Climate records

Because the interpretation turns on whether it is cold enough at the top of the gradient to kill beetles, we assembled the observational record. Hourly observations from the British Columbia Wildfire Service network and daily observations from Environment and Climate Change Canada were retrieved for all stations within 100 km for the winters of the outbreak window. The script in `02.inputs/climate/` streams roughly 2.7 GB and writes the per-station-winter summary the manuscript reads; the fetch cannot sit inside a document render, but every decision about which records to believe is made below, in code.

Two screens matter. Many older Wildfire Service sensors floor at exactly -20.0 °C, so a station-winter whose minimum sits on that floor has an unknown true minimum and is excluded. Isolated spikes, colder than both neighbouring observations by more than 15 °C, are rejected as instrument error during retrieval; one such value, a -40.0 °C daily minimum on a day whose maximum was -4.5 °C, would otherwise have produced exactly the conclusion the record does not support. A second script records the date each station-winter reached its minimum, needed because lethal temperature is conditional on the state of cold-hardening. The window is December to February, which bounds what the record can support.

```{r}
  (panel(terr$Slope,  "(a) Slope", "Degrees", "cividis") |
   panel(terr$TWI,    "(b) Topographic wetness index", "TWI", "mako", -1) |
   panel(terr$RIX,    "(c) Ruggedness", "Index", "rocket", -1)) /
  (panel(terr$TPI600, "(d) Topographic position, 625 m", "TPI (m)", "viridis") |
   panel(terr$HLI,    "(e) Heat load index", "HLI", "inferno") |

fig_terrain
```
